processing: A green tea made in repeated rounds of pan-firing and rolling, described locally as three firings and three rollings: the first softens the leaf, the second straightens it and builds aroma, the third drives off moisture evenly.
harvest_season: Picked in spring and summer. The first pre-Qingming picking is the one local growers make the most of; summer picking also takes place.
appearance_dry: Rolled into twisted strips, as the repeated rolling suggests; little else about the dry leaf is documented.
appearance_liquor: Little is documented; as with other spring pan-fired greens, expect a clear pale yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Little is documented; typical spring greens of this kind open to soft green buds and leaves.
taste_profile: Known above all for an orchid aroma, which rises even during firing. The rest of the cup is thinly described; expect the fresh, gently sweet body typical of high-mountain Sichuan greens.

brewing.notes: General advice for a delicate spring green rather than a local rule: water well off the boil, an open glass or gaiwan, and do not stew it, or the orchid note gets lost.

vintage_note: As is usual for Chinese green teas, it is meant to be bought and drunk from the current year's harvest. Pre-Qingming lots are the first of the season; summer picking is a separate, later tea, so ask which one you are buying.
description:
Guosheng tea comes from Guosheng township in Yanbian County, in the far south of Sichuan near Panzhihua. It is a mountain green with a protected geographical name, and what sets it apart in local telling is an orchid aroma, unusual for a Chinese green.

The gardens sit high, reported at roughly 1,600 to 2,200 metres, in a mild and rainy climate. The makers describe the craft as three firings and three rollings: the leaf is softened, then straightened and scented, then dried evenly, with rolling in between to tighten it into strips.

There is not much written about how it changes across steeps. Treat it as you would other delicate spring greens: cooler water, short contact, and attention to the aroma from the empty cup.

This is a small local tea, with most of the planted area in Guosheng itself, and it rarely travels far. When buying, look for the township or county on the label and for the picking season, since spring and summer tea are both made.
history:
Little is documented about the tea's early history. Its modern story is one of a township industry built around tea gardens, and of the protected name: a 2007 letter from the Yanbian county government set out the protected area as Yongxing, Guosheng, Hongbao, Qinghe and Wenquan.

Reports describe it as the county's first national geographical indication product. Guosheng township still accounts for about nine tenths of the planted area.
